title: Antonelli fastest in Madrid FP3 as Hamilton and Bearman crash
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli finished fastest in Free Practice 3 from Charles Leclerc ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix, as the session was red flagged twice after crashes for Lewis Hamilton and Ollie Bearman.

The Mercedes driver continued his leading pace from FP2 on Friday by setting the best time in the final one-hour session on Saturday, which was disrupted by 30 minutes due to incidents.

Despite the need for teams and drivers to gather as much information as possible at the new venue ahead of a crucial Qualifying session later on Saturday, it took until five minutes had elapsed before any cars ventured out.

The leading contenders waited even longer in order to get the most representative running possible, including Lando Norris despite missing almost the entirety of FP2 as the Briton's McLaren suffered a gearbox issue.

The reigning World Champion aborted his first flying lap with the soft Pirelli tyre after cutting the chicane at Turn 5, while the Ferraris of Hamilton and Leclerc moved to the top of the times.

Home hero Carlos Sainz just avoided making head-on contact with the barrier at Turn 7, with Williams team mate Alex Albon having earlier glanced the wall on the exit of Turn 20 and breaking a rear track rod.

Antonelli moved to the top of the times as the 20-minute mark was reached, the Mercedes driver posting a 1m 33.664s, before Leclerc lowered the benchmark down to a 1m 33.332s moments later.

Hamilton was on course to usurp his team mate with his next effort, but the seven-time World Champion went head-on into the barrier at the final corner, which brought out the red flag.

The Ferrari driver attempted to recover back to the pits while dragging a broken front wing and a front-right puncture, but pulled off after being told to stop by the team multiple times.

The session time was temporarily stopped for barrier repairs before resuming with just 15 minutes remaining, prompting a flurry of activity as drivers attempted to get up to speed over one lap.

This included Arvid Lindblad, who ventured out for the first time since his crash in FP2 as Racing Bulls rushed to fix a problem on his newly-rebuilt car.

Leclerc immediately improved on his best effort, becoming the first driver to dip below the 1m 33s barrier with a 1m 32.963s, with Antonelli's first attempt falling three tenths short from Oscar Piastri, while George Russell was half a second adrift in fourth.

Norris moved to within one-tenth of Leclerc's leading time on just his third flying lap of the day and with minimal mileage under his belt, before Antonelli set a 1m 32.797s to go top with five minutes remaining.

It remained the fastest time as a second red flag was deployed in the final minute after Bearman crashed his Haas at high-speed through Turn 10, putting his team in a rush against time to be ready for Qualifying.

It meant Antonelli was just over one-tenth clear of Leclerc, with Piastri, Norris, Max Verstappen (Red Bull), Russell (Mercedes), Liam Lawson's Red Bull, Audi's Nico Hulkenberg, Hamilton and the second Audi of Gabriel Bortoleto completing the top 10.

Franco Colapinto was P11 for Alpine, followed by the Haas cars of Esteban Ocon and Bearman, Lindblad and the second Racing Bulls of Yuki Tsunoda.

Pierre Gasly's Alpine was P16 from home hero Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin), Sainz, Lance Stroll (Aston Martin), the Cadillacs of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, and Albon with no time.

title: Stroll set for grid penalty at Spanish Grand Prix
excerpt:
Lance Stroll is set to take a grid penalty at the Spanish Grand Prix after Aston Martin opted to fit a range of new power unit components.

A Technical Delegate’s Report released on Saturday confirmed that Stroll’s AMR26 is now running its fifth internal combustion engine, turbocharger and MGU-K, sixth energy store unit and seventh PU-ANC.

With these elements all exceeding the number allocated to each driver, the Canadian will receive a grid drop; the first time the allocation of any one of the components is exceeded, a 10-place grid penalty will be applied, with the second time this occurs (and so on) resulting in a five-place grid drop.

As such, Stroll is likely to be handed a significant penalty for the first-ever F1 race in Madrid.

There were reliability concerns for Aston Martin on track at the Madring during Friday, with Stroll experiencing a suspected battery issue towards the end of Free Practice 2.

Team mate Fernando Alonso also suffered a clutch problem in the day’s first practice hour, before resuming his programme in the second session.

title: Theophile Nael wins first-ever F3 Madring race
excerpt:
Campos Racing’s Theophile Nael secured his third win of the 2026 FIA Formula 3 season in Madrid, dominating the Sprint Race and securing fastest lap en route to victory.

The Frenchman started from second on the grid, but out-launched reverse grid polesitter James Wharton to take the lead into Turn 1.

The PREMA Racing driver looked to have a move completed into Turn 5 but overshot the chicane and was forced to hand the position back before the end of the lap.

After that, Nael went untroubled and set a string of fastest laps to cap off a dominant win ahead of Wharton and PREMA team mate Alex Powell.

Wharton’s P2 finish was his second podium of the year, while Powell’s P3 finish was his maiden visit to the F3 rostrum in just his second weekend in the Championship.

In the title fight, Ugo Ugochukwu added three potentially important points to his tally. The American driver went onto 129 points and closed the gap to leader Freddie Slater down to 12 ahead of the first Feature Race later on Saturday.

Ugochukwu will start from ninth on the grid, while Slater will go from P17 after a tough Qualifying 1 session.

title: Can Mercedes stay ahead of their rivals at the Madring?
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli continued his fine form in Madrid as he topped the times after Friday practice. But with a red flag causing disruption to everyone’s running, and very little long run data gathered on a brand-new track, it’s still all to play for heading into the weekend…

How good is Antonelli looking?

Pretty good, but that’s no surprise given the form he’s been in all season to be fair. The championship leader, who went from 19th to first at the last round in Italy, looked the more comfortable of the two Mercedes, with Antonelli able to quickly find a groove on the soft tyre in Free Practice 2.

Whether or not he can stay there remains to be seen, as the track is evolving quickly and is only set to get more rubbered in as the weekend progresses.

But given he’s in the best place on Friday, and that he and Mercedes tend to make good steps overnight into the weekend, he is in very good shape.

title: What the teams learned about the Madring after day 1 of running
excerpt:
Formula 1 drivers and teams finally had their first proper taste of the Madring in Friday practice, and it proved to be every bit as challenging as had been anticipated.

Simulation can only do so much, so there was a great deal for everyone to learn, and so many unknowns around set-up, power unit deployment, and tyre management. It was the last item that became a major talking point of the day, with tyre graining cropping up early in the first session.

Overall the verdict from the drivers on the new venue was positive.

“I actually really loved it,” said Pierre Gasly, who finished the day in P11. “It was very exciting. It's a track with a lot of adrenaline. At all the corners you kind of see the walls coming at you very quickly, and you’ve got to be extremely precise in your lines, how much you commit to the corner.

“It definitely has this type of like adrenaline element, which you don't always find, but usually find on a street track. So, pretty cool.

“A lot of high-speed, which is unusual for a street track, and it's kind of a mix between like Jeddah and Monaco all combined together. Always exciting to find a new track, and definitely very exciting driving-wise. Now, hopefully, in the race, we can still find opportunities to overtake.”

“I would say honestly it’s more difficult than some tracks,” said Oscar Piastri, who was P7 in FP2. “There's a lot of sections where you're not really brushing up against the walls, you're kind of turning or heading at them, and then you need to avoid them.

“So it makes things quite challenging. Definitely I think everyone is still getting up to speed. But when you get into a decent rhythm over one lap, it's pretty enjoyable. In race running, it's been a nightmare to try and manage the tyres with graining.

“So a lot of corners have been very difficult. It's been an interesting day. I think we are struggling a little bit for pace. But yeah, hopefully we can find a bit more tomorrow.”

Teams had anticipated that graining might be an issue, but the scale of it came as a shock to the system in FP1, which led to set-up tweaks for the second session.

Russell shares ‘the big question mark’ facing drivers in Madrid

“We thought it was a possibility,” said George Russell. “It's often a possibility on new tarmacs. The grip is very high, but you're sliding quite aggressively. With the deg we had in FP1, a six-stop race would have been the fastest way!

“FP2 was slightly better, and I'm sure the race on Sunday will be better again. But that's the biggest question mark.”

It was interesting to see most teams saving two sets of the C2 hard tyres – only Audi deployed them on Friday – which indicates that they will feature heavily in the race.

Inevitably teams had lots of work to do on setup given the need to find a compromise that works on a track that has so many different types of corners.

Ferrari looked competitive from the very start of FP1, although Team Principal Fred Vasseur cautioned that what matters is how the car behaves in Saturday’s Qualifying session.

“I think the good setup is the setup that will work in in quali, not in free practice,” he said. “We know that we'll have a huge track evolution even during the session. The most important is to anticipate the grip in Q3, and to be ready for Q3. It makes no sense to do the best in free practice, and not in quali.

“It's a challenge that you have approximately all the types of corners of the season, and it's a good exercise for the engineers. But at the end, it's also difficult to estimate what will be the grip evolution between FP3 and quali, and even during quali. It means that energy deployment is complicated with the high-speed section, and I think what will be key is to estimate the pace in Q3.”

While Ferrari looked good, with Charles Leclerc finishing FP2 in second place, Red Bull drivers Max Verstappen and Liam Lawson were less satisfied with progress.

“I think it's better to not be happy during Friday!,” said Pierre Wache, echoing Vasseur’s suggestion that what matters is getting it right for the grip level come Qualifying.

“And there's a lot of work to do on car setup, for sure. Mechanical grip, I think the ride is more challenging than what we thought. It's not as smooth.

“On energy deployment, it's clear that we have a lot of work to do there also. And the tyres grained maybe as expected – I think in FP2 we were a little bit better than FP1, and I think we have to continue in this route.”

Wache agreed that it won’t be easy to get it just right: “I think compromising between corner and deployment, some corners are full throttle, and putting some sliding on the tyres. That's something we have to see. But yeah, it is a challenging one.”

And one of the biggest compromises is finding a set-up that works for the places where you have to jump kerbs and is effective throughout the rest of the track.

“It very difficult,” said Audi sporting director Inaki Rueda. “So the main set-up trade that we have here is between running low and stiff for aero, because you have lots of high-speed corners. And usually these cars, the more stiff and low you get the aero platform, the better it is.

“But you have the trade-off of jumping the kerbs, like jumping the kerb in Turn 2. It's a lot of lap time.

"We cannot not jump it, and of course for that you want a higher car, and more of a rolling car. And so that is where the trade-off is, and the answer is going to be difficult.”

title: F3: Kato and Taponen take pole in Madrid
excerpt:
Taito Kato took his maiden FIA Formula 3 pole position with a superb performance in Qualifying 1 in Madrid, while in Qualifying 2, it was Tuukka Taponen that came out on top.

In the battle for the championship, Ugo Ugochukwu was fourth in Q1 and second in Q2, while Freddie Slater was down in P17 in the opening session, and eighth in the second set of 20 minutes.

In Q1, Kato beat Rodin Motorsport’s Pedro Clerot to the top spot by just 0.012s with a 1:50.535.

Taponen was third ahead of Ugochukwu, while Enzo Deligny rounded out the top five.

With Saturday’s two Sprint Race grids set by the results of the first Qualifying session, PREMA Racing’s James Wharton will start from reverse pole position.

Campos’ Theophile Nael will line-up alongside him on the front row with the second PREMA of Alex Powell in third.

In Qualifying 2, Ugochukwu looked set for his first pole position in Formula 3 until Taponen eclipsed his time by 0.021s with a 1:49.750.

Clerot wound up P3 despite hitting the barrier at the final corner on his last lap. Kato was fourth, with Mattia Colnaghi in fifth.

That wraps up the day’s action with the Sprint Race set for 11:05 local time on Saturday morning. Until then, you can read a full report from today’s FIA Formula 3 Qualifying in Madrid on the official website here.

title: Madring Qualifying 'going to be an exciting one' – Leclerc
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc believes that Qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix this weekend is "going to be an exciting one", having got his first taste of the Madring on Friday.

Ferrari proved to be Mercedes' closest challenger during the opening day of practice at Formula 1's newest venue, which provided plenty of challenges for teams and drivers.

Leclerc finished P3 and P2 in the two, one-hour sessions and was just one-tenth behind Free Practice 2 pacesetter Kimi Antonelli after a positive day behind the wheel.

"It has been a very interesting day. Obviously it is a completely new track for everyone. It is a very, very challenging track and I think for Qualifying, it is going to be an exciting one," said Leclerc.

"Lots of work ahead of us to try and improve the car for tomorrow but I think the day went quite well. I think we went through our programme, which is important.

"We did maximise the amount of laps we could do which was also one of the main targets for today, being on a new track. Looking forward to tomorrow to try and do something good in Qualifying."

Leclerc has generally been strong on street circuits during his F1 career, but admits that he doesn't have a target in mind during Saturday's crucial Qualifying session, with overtaking likely to be difficult in Madrid.

"It is more about trying to maximise what we have and we will see at the end of Qualifying where that leaves us," he said.

"I expect the Mercedes is quite strong but you never know so I’ll just focus on myself, trying to optimise everything we can on our car and hopefully we can do something really good tomorrow."

Team mate Lewis Hamilton also showed strong pace, finishing P4 and P3, but Ferrari team boss Fred Vassuer is wary of the team's prospects so early into the weekend.

In particular, that the track's condition will only improve and move the goalposts that teams have calibrated to on Friday.

"I think we are far away of the lap time of Quali, the most important is to improve the competitiveness of the car and for the driver to understand the track also," said Vasseur.

"I think there is a lot of topic about energy deployment and so, that means racing is open and everybody will improve a lot. We just have to be focused on ourselves.

"I think we are all in the same boat, that track evolution is huge from one session to the other one, but almost from one lap to the other one balance is changing a little bit."

title: Oliver Bearman ruled out of F1 qualifying after heavy FP3 shunt
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman will not take part in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix after his crash at the end of the final free practice session.

Haas was unable to sufficiently repair his car in time for the grid-setting session at the Madring, which means the British driver will start Sunday's race from the rear of the field.

The 21-year-old found the wall at Turn 11 with less than a minute of FP3 remaining, a session in which he finished P13, half a tenth adrift of team-mate Esteban Ocon.

Minutes before qualifying was due to get underway, the boards were up at the Haas driver's garage, and little work appeared to be happening on his car.

Just as the session got going, the American team confirmed the inevitable.

"Ollie Bearman will not participate in qualifying for the Spanish Grand Prix as a result of the damage sustained to his VF-26," the team said.

It is not yet clear what the extent of the repairs that will need to take place are, but if a chassis change has been required, Bearman would not have been able to take part in qualifying anyway, as the team would have to self-scutineer, and that process cannot be done between sessions.

title: McLaren pushing to accelerate Max Verstappen ally's Red Bull exit - report
excerpt:
McLaren is in talks with Red Bull to bring forward Gianpiero Lambiase's move to Woking, according to reports.

The development means Max Verstappen could be without his trusted race engineer for as many as three race weekends towards the tail end of the F1 season.

It was confirmed earlier this year that Lambiase will leave Red Bull for McLaren no later than 2028, where he will take on the role of chief racing officer under team principal Andrea Stella.

At Red Bull, Lambiase served as both head of racing and Verstappen's race engineer throughout the Dutchman's championship-winning years.

Tom Hart being readied as Verstappen's new engineer

From next season, Tom Hart will step in as Verstappen's permanent race engineer. Hart is already being prepared for the role, and RacingNews365 understands he will take full charge of three race weekends in 2026, understood to be Austin, Brazil and Las Vegas.

He was previously given his first outing alongside Verstappen during a practice session at Monza.

Beyond the Hart preparations, De Telegraaf reports that McLaren is actively pushing to shorten Lambiase's gardening leave period.

The team are said to be reluctant for him to sit at home for an entire year before joining, prompting Zak Brown to open discussions with Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies over an earlier start date.

The expectation now is that Lambiase will no longer be in Red Bull employment by 2027.

Red Bull have already moved to fill the void on the management side, recently confirming the signing of Tom McCullough as the new head of racing.

The Briton arrives from Aston Martin and slots directly into the role Lambiase vacated within the leadership structure around Mekies.

title: 2026 Spanish Grand Prix - F2 Madrid Sprint Race results
excerpt:
Check out the full F2 Sprint Race results from Madrid in support of the 2026 F1 Spanish Grand Prix.

Ritomo Miyata claimed his first Formula 2 victory in a Spanish sprint which had huge effects on the title race.

The sole Hitech in the field after Colton Herta's withdrawal, Miyata eased to a breakthrough victory, but the biggest drama centred around championship leader Nikola Tsolov.

Tucked up behind Campos team-mate Noel Leon, Tsolov requested to be let through into fourth place to ease ahead of title rival Rafael Camara, who was running in sixth to earn more points than the Ferrari junior.

However, Campos did not issue the instruction, meaning Tsolov remained behind Leon until he clipped a wall in the final sector and stalled the car, leading to a DNF.

This then gave Camara a perfect opportunity to reduce the 11-point gap to Tsolov, which he did with a sixth-placed finish, earning three points, thus holding 169 points to Tsolov's 177, a deficit of eight.

Emerson Fittipaldi Jr and Laurens van Hoepen completed the Sprint podium.

title: Toto Wolff strikes back at 'couch warriors' with 'complete bullshit' defence
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has dismissed suggestions that George Russell was disadvantaged by Mercedes' decision to pit Kimi Antonelli under the virtual safety car at the Italian Grand Prix, calling the criticism from "couch warriors" as "complete bullshit".

Antonelli won at Monza from Russell, the pair finishing 3.8s apart to complete a Mercedes one-two at the championship leader's home race. It extended Antonelli's lead in the drivers' standings to 66 points over his team-mate, with Mercedes now 122 clear of Ferrari in the constructors' championship.

The flashpoint was the mid-race virtual safety car period, which allows a car to be pitted at a reduced time loss because track speeds fall while the pit lane limit stays the same. Mercedes brought in Antonelli, who had started on the hard tyre and switched to the medium.

Russell, already running hards, was in the lead from Antonelli and stayed out. Pirelli had gone into the weekend expecting a one-stop to be the likely route at Monza, with rear tyre temperatures the main thing to manage rather than outright degradation.

Asked whether Russell should have had priority in the call, the Mercedes team principal was blunt.

Discussing questions raised as to whether Russell should have had priority in the decision-making in Monza, Wolff replied to Sky F1: "No, it's absolutely the right thing we did.

"He was on the hards; it was predicted to be a one-stop as the better strategy. The medium was a compromise. We had to put the medium on Kimi because he started on the hards.

"There is just no way, and obviously there are some couch warriors that will drop their comments after having watched some other material online, saying that he [Russell] was penalised.

"It's complete bullshit. Sorry, I should say that it's complete crap."

Wolff wary of Spanish GP qualifying 'yo-yo' threat

Wolff was speaking after final practice in Madrid, where Antonelli again set the pace. The 20-year-old lapped the Circuito de Madring in 1m 32.797 to head Charles Leclerc by 0.166s, with Russell only sixth, 0.702s adrift.

Looking ahead to qualifying, Wolff said: "I think if we put it all together, we fight for pole and we fight for the first row.

"But it could be a little bit of yo-yoing. It could be all within a tenth. So you could be on the good side of it or on the wrong side."

title: Full Ferrari-Lewis Hamilton radio disagreement revealed as clear demand ignored
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton deliberately disobeyed multiple instructions from his race engineer, Carlo Santi, to stop his Ferrari on track after sustaining significant damage to his car during FP3 at the Spanish Grand Prix.

The seven-time F1 drivers' champion crashed at the final corner at the Madring, bringing out a red flag around 25 minutes into the final hour of free practice running.

Having been able to reverse his SF-26 out of the barriers, the British driver attempted to nurse it back to the pit lane and avoid missing out on the final half an hour of the session.

However, with the front wing of his car tucked up underneath the floor, he was ordered to pull to one side, as it was in an unsafe condition to drive.

For over half the lap, Hamilton went against the instructions, despite being told that the race director, Rui Marques, had requested he stop at the safest possible place.

It was initially feared that he might face repercussions for his actions, but the 41-year-old has yet to be noted by the stewards in Madrid, so he may avoid further investigation and punishment.

At the Canadian Grand Prix, Sergio Perez was handed a three-place grid penalty for the next round after driving his Red Bull in an unsafe condition.

Check out the full conversation between Santi and Hamilton over Ferrari team radio below!

Full Ferrari team radio transcript

Carlo Santi: "Mode warm-up, mode warm-up, please."

Santi: "If you are stuck, switch off. If you are stuck, switch off."

[Hamilton starts moving]

Santi: "Stop the car, stop the car, stop the car."

Lewis Hamilton: "The car is going."

[keeps going]

Santi: "You have the wing under the wheels. Stop in the safest place, the safest place possible, as soon as you see the gate."

Hamilton: "If I can make it back, I will. If I can't, I'll do it safely."

[keeps going]

Santi: "We have a puncture on the front right. Stop the car."

Hamilton: "I can see that. I can see that."

[keeps going]

Santi: "Stop... stop the car at the first gate you find. It's the race director; he's asking to stop the car in the safest place possible."

Hamilton: "I can make it back safely!"

Santi: "They told us, they told us, it's a formal request; they told us to stop in the safest place possible. Stop before Turn 12, on the left." Santi: "Stop on the track right."

Hamilton: "But I can make it back— okay, I'm stopping the car."

Santi: "Ignition off and PO, please. Ignition off and PO."

title: Colton Herta withdraws from F2 sprint due to illness
excerpt:
Colton Herta has been forced to withdraw from the Formula 2 sprint race in Madrid after falling ill on the morning of the event.

Hitech confirmed the news on social media ahead of Saturday's race at the new Madring circuit, stating: "Colton Herta has withdrawn from today's Formula 2 Sprint Race in Madrid after feeling unwell."

It is a setback the American can ill afford. Herta sits 17th in the F2 standings with just 26 points after 10 of 14 rounds, and every missed opportunity to score makes his task that much harder with only four rounds remaining.

The 2026 season was always going to test Herta. He left IndyCar, where he had been a regular frontrunner, to join Hitech as part of a broader move into the Cadillac F1 programme.

The objective was to accumulate FIA Super Licence points and ultimately make his case for a future F1 seat. However, it has not gone to plan.

After a promising start, scoring points in each of the first three feature races, his form has tailed off significantly.

Herta himself has described the campaign as "pretty disappointing," admitting that "the results are disappointing. There's no hiding from it."

His Monza weekend, the round before Madrid, saw him crash in practice, qualify P20 and retire from the feature race after going off at Parabolica.

Whether Herta will be fit to compete in Sunday's feature race at the Madring remains to be seen.

Due to the temporary suspension of the session in FP3 caused by Lewis Hamilton's red flag, the F2 sprint race has been delayed, with the formation lap now scheduled to start at 14:35 local time.

title: Lewis Hamilton disobeys Ferrari orders as Kimi Antonelli reigns supreme in double-red flagged FP3
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli went fastest in the final free practice session at the Spanish Grand Prix, besting Charles Leclerc by almost two-tenths of a second in Madrid.

Oscar Piastri went third-quickest at the all-new Madring, ahead of Lando Norris and Max Verstappen in a twice-stopped and extended FP3.

Lewis Hamilton, who finished down in ninth, caused the second red flag of the F1 portion of the weekend in the Spanish capital, after crashing into the barriers on the outside of the final corner with just under 25 minutes gone.

After a 20-minute delay, the FIA opted to temporarily suspend the session with a quarter of an hour remaining, in order to prevent further loss of running.

The Ferrari driver, having attempted to limp back around to the pits with the front wing of his SF-26 tucked up beneath it, repeatedly ignored instructions from the Scuderia's pit wall to park up, which came after formal requests from the race director.

He eventually complied, but the stewards may take a dim view of his actions. Having been denied the opportunity to end the session and having damaged his car, the officials could decide to hand him a sporting punishment, which could be as severe as a grid penalty.

However, Hamilton has yet to be noted, so he may conceivably avoid any investigation into the incident.

With less than a minute remaining, Ollie Bearman found the wall at Turn 11, bringing out another red flag and ending the session.

Check out the full FP3 report from the Spanish Grand Prix at the Madring below!

Lewis Hamilton disobeys Ferrari orders as Kimi Antonelli reigns supreme in double-red flagged FP3

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

First third

Following his shunt in FP2, Arvid Lindblad would have a late start to the final hour of practice. Racing Bulls, despite changing the chassis on his car, opted not to break curfew last night, meaning the team's mechanics had a busy morning.

However, the British driver would not initially miss much, with the circuit remaining characteristically quiet to start FP3.

It would be over five minutes before the first driver would emerge. Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto ventured out to get the ball rolling, soon to be joined by team-mate Nico Hulkenberg.

On medium tyres, both put in 1:35.7s to begin, some way off the ultimate pace seen on the first day of running.

Interestingly, the German team opted to use a set of hard tyres for each driver on Friday, whereas all other teams did not touch the white-walled Pirellis. Will that prove to be a strategic masterstroke later in the weekend?

Alex Albon lightly hit the wall in the final sector with around 15 minutes on the clock, but it was enough for him to return his Williams to the pits for a closer inspection. The Grove-based team later confirmed the contact at the rear-left corner had ended his session, due to a broken rear axle and suspension.

With the entire field bar Verstappen and Lindblad having come out on circuit, Ferrari would leave the way as the session approached the 20-minute mark. However, Hamilton's 1:34.284 was still some six-tenths off Antonelli's best time from FP2.

Soon after, the Mercedes driver would bring the hammer down further, going just two milliseconds shy of his aforementioned best time on Friday.

Sainz, in the second FW48, had a sketchy near-miss into the uphill Turn 7, braking heavily and locking up to narrowly avoid hitting the wall head-on.

Midpoint of the session

Seconds after the session ticked past the 20-minute mark, Leclerc posted the quickest time of the weekend so far, +0.330 faster than Antonelli's FP2 time, with a 1:33.332.

Hamilton would trigger the second F1 red flag of the weekend soon after, crashing his Ferrari at the final corner. Despite getting the SF-26 going again, the stoppage had already been triggered.

With his front wing caught under his car, the seven-time F1 drivers' champion was clearly instructed by the Scuderia to park up, putting an end to his session.

However, he would ignore those orders for over half the lap, insisting he could make it back to the pits for the final half an hour of running.

He eventually acquiesced to the Italian team's demands, but put himself at risk of further punishment from the stewards for driving in an unsafe condition.

With potential floor damage as well, Hamilton now faced the worst of both worlds, having lost any opportunity to do late-session qualifying simulations.

Final 15

With the clock stopped at 15:38 left to run after the FIA decided to halt proceedings, the session resumed two minutes after it was originally scheduled to end, at 13:32 local time.

Verstappen, having only completed two reconnaissance laps to that point, was eager to get going, and immediately went third fastest.

The delay worked in Lindblad's favour. The Racing Bulls driver emerged for the first time in the session, having been aided by the session suspension.

Leclerc remained top as the times came tumbling down, the nine-time grand prix winner dipping into the 1:32s, with a 1:32.963.

Half a second separated the top six, with both McLarens and Mercedes joining Verstappen, who brought up the rear of that group.

However, the times would continue to drop in the final few moments of the extended session, with Antonelli ultimately conquering FP3.

With under a minute remaining, Bearman crashed heavily at Turn 11, destroying his Haas and putting his participation in qualifying later under threat.

title: Lewis Hamilton facing double punishment after blatantly ignoring Ferrari instructions
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton faces a double punishment after blatantly ignoring instructions from Ferrari, following a costly accident during final practice ahead of the Spanish Grand Prix.

The seven-time world champion was on a hot lap but went into the barrier at the final corner. Hamilton entered too hot and went straight into the barrier, breaking his front wing.

It triggered an immediate red flag. Hamilton reversed out of the barrier and escaped suspension damage, attempting to bring his damaged SF-26 back to the garage.

The front wing scrapped along the track surface, causing a puncture as it became stuck underneath the front wheels.

Ferrari instructed Hamilton to stop the car but the Briton refused on multiple occasions, before eventually coming to a halt.

Not only does the 41-year-old now miss the rest of third practice and crucial qualifying simulations, he will likely face a punishment for driving a damaged car.

title: Racing Bulls in race against time with Arvid Lindblad
excerpt:
Arvid Lindblad was left facing an anxious wait to see how much track action he would see in final practice for the Spanish Grand Prix.

Around F1's newest circuit, the Madring in the north-east of the Spanish capital of Madrid, Lindblad was the only driver to spark a red flag across the two hour-long sessions on Friday.

The 22-corner Madring had been predicted in the build-up to cause chaos given the nature of the track.

But it was not until FP2 was 35 minutes old that the maiden stoppage occurred, with Lindblad, who has impressed in his rookie season with Racing Bulls, losing the rear end of his car into the fast Turn 13 left-hander.

Trying to hold the slide, the rear of the car initially hit a TecPro barrier, with the front following suit, leaving his mechanics with a major overnight repair job.

The damage was bad enough to spark a chassis change. The FIA confirmed shortly before the start of FP3 that the team had duly completed the scrutineering declaration form for Lindblad's car after a survival cell change.

As the session started, the Racing Bulls mechanics were seen frantically working on Lindblad's car.

title: Oliver Bearman spots 'oversight' in new Madrid F1 track layout
excerpt:
Oliver Bearman has spotted what he believes to be an "oversight" in the track design for the new Spanish Grand Prix venue in Madrid.

The Madring becomes the 79th circuit to host a world championship grand prix this weekend with the new 22-turn 3.3-mile layout around the IFEMA entertainment complex near to the Real Madrid training centre.

The semi-permanent street track is expected to be a major challenge, with Turn 12 in particular, La Monumental, a huge banked right-hander in the middle of the lap.

Overtaking is expected to be a challenge, with the high number of 90-degree 'point and squirt' corners, especially in the second-half of the lap, with overtaking set to be difficult with so few opportunities.

One such place is into Turn 5, at the end of the first SM-mode straight, but as Haas driver Bearman has pointed out, the braking zone into the left-right-left chicane that follows is curved - thus limiting chances for a move to be successfully made.

"It seems to be a track where it's going to be a big challenge to overtake, and it is a shame in a way because I think the layout is okay," Bearman told media, including RacingNews365.

"But there are some features of the circuit which naturally deter overtaking. One of them is the braking for Turn 5, which is curved, and that's the real overtaking opportunity, and that curved braking takes away any possibility of different lines and sending one up the inside.

"So that's a shame and maybe a bit of an oversight, but it means that we're going to be fully focused on qualifying, and to do a good qualifying, of course, you need full confidence, and that starts from your first lap on Friday.

"I think it's going to be one of those races where we're very much focused on qualifying, similar to Budapest, Monaco, or even Zandvoort.

"In the simulator, you don't drive around with the fear of hurting yourself or the car, so the goal of the sim is to try and hit every wall possible in a way, because like that you learn exactly where the limits are and you find them in the most efficient way possible, and by doing that, you don't do that on the real track.

"It's definitely a tough track. But every street track I go to on the sim, it's pretty normal that you're bouncing off the walls quite a lot because that's the beauty of the simulator."

title: Charles Leclerc in agreement with Fernando Alonso over new Spanish GP circuit
excerpt:
Charles Leclerc has agreed with Fernando Alonso's assessment of the new Spanish Grand Prix track in that it will heavily favour qualifying, with overtaking likely to be incredibly difficult in Sunday's race.

On initial inspection following Friday's two practice sessions, the 22-corner circuit situated in the north-east of the Spanish capital, Madrid, is incredibly challenging for the drivers.

What was also evident is that there appear to be precious few overtaking opportunities, ensuring qualifying and a good grid slot will be paramount.

Ferrari at least appeared to be on the pace, with Leclerc and team-mate Lewis Hamilton second and third quickest, both just over a tenth of a second adrift of Kimi Antonelli in his Mercedes.

Prior to practice, Leclerc described the circuit as "very challenging", albeit one he enjoys as a driver.

On the downside, he added: "I think come Sunday, the amount of overtaking opportunities will be very little.

"In qualifying, it will be a very cool and challenging track for all drivers. And for that I'm looking forward to it."

[Article continues below]

Leclerc reveals priority shift

Assessing Alonso's comment that qualifying will be better than the race, Leclerc added: "It's the kind of weekend where you want to focus more on the qualifying pace than on the race pace.

"Come Sunday, I feel like it's going to be difficult, apart from at the start, to gain positions.

"For sure, our priority will be to try and maximise practice to make sure that in Q3 we end up with the right car and with a good lap.

"So yeah, the priority will be shifted a little bit more towards qualifying. I still think the race can be interesting with the strategy, but maybe the overtaking will be a bit less than at other tracks."
